newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China seen tightening noose around Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: China seen tightening noose around Taiwan.

text.p: Taiwan's foreign minister failed to save ties with South Africa and saw a mission to Belgium reduced to a fruitless stopover in signs that China's diplomatic noose around the island was tightening, analysts said on Monday.

John Chang's Johannesburg visit -- which began last Tuesday in the hope of salvaging ties but ended four days later with the angry recall of Taiwan's ambassador to Pretoria -- showed that China was slamming the international door on Taipei and keeping it tightly shut, analysts said.
They said Chang's hastily arranged subsequent visit to Belgium on Sunday was but a symbolic, and even desperate, gesture that had no realistic diplomatic purpose.

"John Chang went to South Africa hoping to talk South Africa out of its decision to recognise Beijing, and Pretoria simply said a very clear no," said Lu Ya-li, a political science professor at the National Taiwan University.
"The government has got to realise by now how much pressure foreign governments are feeling from China," Lu said.
South African President Nelson Mandela announced on November 27 that Pretoria, the biggest of Taiwan's 30 diplomatic allies, would switch ties to Beijing in 1997.

China demands that nations sever relations with Taiwan as the price for diplomatic ties with Beijing. China regards Taiwan as a rebel province and seeks to isolate it completely in the international arena.

Despite Mandela's pledge to maintain close relations at an unofficial level, Chang angrily announced during his Pretoria visit on Thursday that Taiwan would recall its ambassador and suspend all aid projects and treaties.
A chastened Chang left South Africa on Saturday and headed secretly for Belgium, with Taiwan media painting his extended foreign journey as a mysterious diplomatic mission with a secret agenda.

Officials had said Chang would visit several countries "to strengthen our relations", but by Monday the Foreign Ministry said he was visiting only Belgium and characterised the trip as a "transit stop" rather than one with official goals.
Chang himself said on Sunday in Belgium that his visit was "unofficial" but insisted it had "diplomatic interests".
In an indication Chang's mission had crashed before taking off, Vice Foreign Minister Cheng Chien-jen said Chang would return to Taiwan as early as Tuesday afternoon.

"The trip to Belgium simply did not make any sense other than Chang trying to save face and make it look like Taipei is doing something to counter Beijing," said Tim Ting, political analyst at National Taiwan University.
"It was unrealistic for him to meet any officials on such short notice. The whole thing was just a show to salvage some pride from the failure in South Africa," Ting added.
Taiwan newspapers said Chang cut short and toned down his Belgium visit amid pressure from China, which has formal ties with Brussels.
The squeeze was so tight that several Belgian officials even cancelled a round of golf with Chang, Taipei's China Times newspaper said.
Luo Zhi-zhen, a politics professor at Soochow University, said Taiwan had no choice but to maintain a tough stance to avoid being driven completely from the diplomatic scene.

"Taipei knew that recalling an ambassador and stopping at Belgium would not change the picture, but the government has to act tough because if it fails to assert itself, other allies are going to leave also," Luo said.
Taiwan's 30 diplomatic allies are mostly impoverished states in Africa and Central America.
